overview: Maiasaura peeblesorum ("good mother lizard") transformed understanding of dinosaur parental behaviour. From the Late Cretaceous Two Medicine Formation of Montana (~76 Ma), nesting colonies preserving eggs, hatchlings and juveniles at different stages were discovered by Jack Horner and Bob Makela in 1978. The hatchlings' underdeveloped limb bones showed they were born helpless and required parental feeding in the nest — the first evidence of extended parental care in non-avian dinosaurs.

The Maiasaura bonebeds in Montana are extraordinary: a single catastrophic event — possibly a volcanic ashfall — killed approximately 10,000 individuals in one horizon. This mass-death assemblage across a wide area provides bone histology data for the entire population, showing Maiasaura grew at rates comparable to modern large mammals rather than reptiles.

articles.title: The discovery that changed palaeontology
articles.body: Jack Horner and Bob Makela described Maiasaura in 1979 from material found by Marion Brandvold near Choteau, Montana in 1978. The eggs and hatchlings showed underdeveloped legs and worn teeth — indicating the young were fed in the nest by adults for an extended period. This overturned the prevailing view of dinosaurs as indifferent egg-layers and established them as attentive parents.

articles.title: Growth rates
articles.body: Bone histology from the massive Two Medicine bonebed shows that Maiasaura grew from 50 cm at hatching to 7 metres adult length in 6–8 years — a rate comparable to modern large ungulates, not reptiles. This is now considered typical for hadrosaurs and confirms that non-avian dinosaurs had elevated metabolic rates relative to modern reptiles.

articles.title: Hadrosaur ecology
articles.body: Maiasaura was a flat-headed (non-crested) hadrosaur that lived in large herds on the coastal plains of the Western Interior Seaway. It migrated seasonally — bone evidence suggests the Two Medicine Formation records different herd stages at different times of year. The colonial nesting, where multiple females laid eggs in the same area, mirrors modern colonial nesters such as penguins.

facts: Nest colonies and very young individuals in nests show repeated nesting-site use and extended nest occupancy.
The evidence is consistent with parental care but does not specify which sex cared for young or every detail of provisioning.
Large growth-series samples document rapid growth and population structure.

animalParagraphs: Maiasaura was a medium to large hadrosaurid, with adults roughly seven to nine metres long. It had a broad, flat-headed skull with a small solid crest in front of the eyes, a wide beak and grinding dental batteries. Hatchlings were less than half a metre long, and bone histology shows that they grew rapidly, approaching adult size within about eight years.

It is famous for the nesting grounds discovered near Choteau, Montana, in 1978. Nests containing hatchlings with worn teeth but poorly ossified limb joints indicated that young stayed in the nest and were fed, evidence that gave the genus its name. The record supports extended nest occupancy and repeated use of the same nesting sites, though the sex of the caring parent and the details of provisioning are not known.

Elsewhere in the Two Medicine Formation, a bonebed containing the remains of thousands of individuals killed together preserves a cross-section of a population. Sampling of that bonebed has produced one of the most detailed growth and survivorship records for any dinosaur.
animalHighlights: Nest colonies with eggs, embryos and nest-bound hatchlings, the first strong evidence of extended parental care in a dinosaur.
A growth series from embryo to adult showing rapid early growth and near-adult size in under a decade.
A flat, broad skull with a small solid crest above the snout, unlike the hollow crests of lambeosaurine relatives.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Dental batteries and tooth wear show grinding of tough plants; worn teeth in hatchlings indicate that nestlings ate plant material too.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Limb anatomy allows both gaits, and growth changes suggest juveniles were more bipedal than adults. Habitual speed is inferred.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Adult lengths come from bonebed material; masses of a few tonnes are model-based estimates.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Skull and body proportions are known at every growth stage, but skin, colour and any soft crest are not preserved for this genus.

locality.name: Willow Creek Anticline and Egg Mountain
locality.note: The nesting grounds and type material come from exposures of the Two Medicine Formation west of Choteau. The large bonebed lies elsewhere in the same formation.

presentation.classificationSummary: Maiasaura is a saurolophine hadrosaurid within Brachylophosaurini, a group of flat-headed duck-billed dinosaurs with small solid crests that also includes Brachylophosaurus. Its position is consistent across recent analyses.

related.reason: Compare with its closest well-known relative, a solid-crested hadrosaurid from Montana and Alberta.
Compare with a hollow-crested hadrosaurid also known from eggs and embryos in the Two Medicine Formation.

questions.title: How exactly were the young cared for?
questions.copy: Nest-bound hatchlings show that adults attended nests, but which sex did so, whether food was brought or regurgitated, and how long care lasted are inferences.

questions.title: What killed the bonebed population?
questions.copy: The mass-death assemblage may record a single catastrophic event or a combination of events, which affects how its population structure is read.

questions.title: How many species are there?
questions.copy: Only Maiasaura peeblesorum is recognised. Whether all Two Medicine material belongs to one species has not been fully tested at specimen level.

review.ageReviewNote: The Two Medicine Maiasaura record is late Campanian, approximately 76.7-75 Ma.

panel.headline: Eggs, nests, hatchlings and thousands of bones from one Montana rock unit.
panel.standfirst: Maiasaura is known from nesting colonies, embryos, hatchlings, juveniles and adults, and from a bonebed containing the remains of thousands of individuals. Few dinosaurs are documented across so much of their life cycle.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is known from many individuals at every growth stage, from embryo to adult, together with eggs and nests.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Skulls and skeletons of adults and juveniles, embryos and hatchlings within nests, eggs and eggshell, and bonebed material representing all skeletal regions across the growth series.
knownRemains.note: The name-bearing specimen is a partial adult skull. Much of the vast bonebed material is disarticulated, so complete individual skeletons are rarer than the sheer number of bones suggests.

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Nests with eggs, embryos and hatchlings, and skeletal material from every growth stage, all from the Two Medicine Formation.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A colonial nester whose hatchlings stayed in the nest and were cared for, growing rapidly to adult size; a herbivore that may have moved in large groups.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Which parent provided care and how, colour and skin, the cause of the bonebed mortality, and whether every referred specimen is one species.
